tagline: Coastal forests, bluff-top curves and beach towns between Taholah and Hoquiam.
intro: Hidden Coast Scenic Byway follows SR 109 between Taholah and Hoquiam, winding through coastal forest and beach communities. The road climbs ocean-facing bluffs and weaves between small canyons and ravines near Copalis Beach. It is a Washington state scenic byway; State of Washington Tourism highlights wide sandy beaches, ocean views and places sharing the Quinault Indian Nation’s culture. The tourism organization gives the drive 41 miles and an hour and a half.

An early automobile road linked Hoquiam, Moclips and Taholah by an inland alignment with connections to Copalis Beach. In 1947, Secondary State Highway 9C shifted to run west from Hoquiam to Ocean City, then north to the reservation boundary beyond Moclips. The 1964 highway renumbering gave it the SR 109 name. Plans to extend the highway north from Taholah toward Queets date to the mid-twentieth century. Work on a segment began in the 1960s but stopped because of access issues; the proposed coastal connection remains unbuilt.

Traveling south from Taholah, follow Grenville Bay through forest to Moclips, then Pacific Beach and Seabrook. Beyond Copalis Beach and Ocean City, the road turns inland along the north side of Grays Harbor, passing cranberry bogs. Brackenridge Bluff and Bowerman Basin mark the approach to Hoquiam.

moments.title: Taholah
moments.text: Taholah is the Quinault Indian Nation’s headquarters near the mouth of the Quinault River. The village lies within a tsunami inundation zone. Its 2,000-foot seawall has needed repeated repairs after breaches; the Army Corps of Engineers raised it four feet in 2014 in response to more frequent flooding. The tribal government proposed relocating the village uphill in 2015, and construction began in 2019. In May 2021, the Generations Building opened as the first part of the relocated village, serving seniors and children. The Nation also owns and funds the Quinault Cultural Center and Museum in Taholah.

moments.title: Moclips
moments.text: Two different Moclips Beach Hotels occupied the same site in the space of two years. Dr. Edward Lycan’s first hotel was built in 1905 with 150 rooms, then burned within months. The replacement, completed in 1907, rose three stories and stretched a block long. It advertised 270 outside rooms and 2,000 feet of covered veranda. The growing town also supported canneries and the M.R. Smith Lumber and Shingle Mill. Fatal storms in 1911 washed away much of Moclips and left the hotel in pieces. By the end of 1913 it was gone. The community lies near the Moclips River’s mouth.

moments.title: Copalis Beach
moments.text: Commercial diggers took more than a million pounds of shellfish from Copalis Beach during 1947 and 1948. Tourists dug thousands of pounds more. Razor-clam digging remains a seasonal activity here, alongside miles of open beach. At the Copalis River’s mouth, Griffiths-Priday State Park includes low dunes and both ocean and freshwater shorelines. Its Copalis Spit is a small peninsula that provides refuge for migrating birds.
moments.notice: Low dunes and the Copalis Spit mark the river-mouth landscape at Griffiths-Priday State Park.
